title: Real-rank hyperoperation uniqueness
W: Find natural rules that single out exactly one way to fill in operations between addition, multiplication and exponentiation, and prove exactly one family obeys them.
M: Let $a>1$ and $F_s(b)=a[s]b$ for $s\in[1,3]$, $b>0$, with $F_1(b)=a+b$, $F_2(b)=ab$, $F_3(b)=a^b$ and $F_{s+1}(b+1)=F_s(F_{s+1}(b))$ for $s\in[1,2]$. Find natural extra conditions (analyticity in $(s,b)$ plus a convexity condition in $s$) under which exactly one such family exists, and prove it.
why: Interpolating integer-indexed operations to real rank is a well-known folklore problem. A Bohr–Mollerup-type uniqueness theorem would settle it the way log-convexity settles the Gamma function.
issues: As submitted, M is not a precise statement: it does not say what the recursion law is, what log-convexity means, or what is log-convex. The recursion also only makes sense for s in [1,2]. Given F_s on [1,2], F_{s+1} is a fractional iterate of F_s, so it is fixed only up to the choice of fractional iteration. The whole of [1,2] is then a free family between a+b and ab, and one scalar convexity condition cannot plausibly pin it down. Finding the right axioms is the open problem itself, not a gap in the wording. Ill-posed as stated; the repaired M above is a research programme, not a definite question.

title: Hearing tetrahedra
W: Triangles can be heard: their Dirichlet spectrum determines them up to congruence (Durso 1988; Grieser–Maronna 2013). Show the same for tetrahedra.
M: Let $T_1,T_2\subset\mathbb R^3$ be (nondegenerate) tetrahedra whose Dirichlet Laplacian eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, coincide. Prove that $T_1$ and $T_2$ are congruent.
why: This is the natural next case of Kac's question after triangles. The heat-trace invariants of a polyhedron (volume, surface area, an edge sum weighted by dihedral angles, vertex terms) give about four numbers, but a tetrahedron has six degrees of freedom, so a proof would need new input from the wave trace or periodic billiard orbits in 3D polyhedra. It would be the first 'hearable' class of 3D polyhedra with more than a few parameters.
issues: Tried the heat-invariant count: 4 invariants against 6 parameters, so the heat trace cannot be enough; the problem is not trivial. Found no proof and no isospectral counterexample. The surveys found (Grieser–Maronna, Rowlett et al.) state the polygon/triangle results and do not list tetrahedra as solved. Likely a known folklore question, so novelty is low. Added 'with multiplicity'.

title: Sup norms on the Fermat quartic
W: On a round sphere, some eigenfunctions pile up at the poles as much as is possible. Show this cannot happen on the surface x⁴+y⁴+z⁴=1.
M: Let $S=\{x^4+y^4+z^4=1\}\subset\mathbb R^3$ with the induced metric, and let $\Delta\varphi=-\lambda\varphi$, $\|\varphi\|_{L^2(S)}=1$. Prove $\sup_{\varphi}\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty(S)}=o(\lambda^{1/4})$ as $\lambda\to\infty$. Equivalently (Sogge–Zelditch), prove that $S$ has no pole: no point $p$ such that every geodesic from $p$ comes back to $p$ as a smoothly closed geodesic.
why: Sogge–Zelditch showed that a real-analytic surface has maximal eigenfunction growth only if it has a pole. Proving that explicit surfaces have no pole is the missing step for concrete examples; the triaxial ellipsoid is already done.
issues: By Sogge–Zelditch II (arXiv 1409.2063), S is real-analytic, so the problem reduces exactly to showing S has no pole. That is a purely dynamical question about geodesics, probably checkable by rigorous numerics plus symmetry. The choice of surface is arbitrary; it is a second instance of a method already used for ellipsoids. Clarified the eigenvalue convention: λ^{1/4} with λ the eigenvalue is the sharp exponent.

title: Is the Petersen graph common?
W: Color the edges of a huge complete graph red and blue. Does a random coloring minimize the number of single-color copies of the Petersen graph?
M: Let $P$ be the Petersen graph ($10$ vertices, $15$ edges) and $m(P)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\min_{\chi}\frac{\#\{\text{monochromatic copies of }P\text{ in }(K_n,\chi)\}}{\#\{\text{copies of }P\text{ in }K_n\}}$, minimum over red/blue colorings $\chi$ of $E(K_n)$. Is $m(P)=2^{-14}$, i.e. is $P$ common? Equivalently, is $t(P,W)+t(P,1-W)\ge 2^{-14}$ for every graphon $W$? If not, determine $m(P)$.
why: Which graphs are common (random coloring is optimal) is a central question in Ramsey multiplicity. The known obstructions (containing $K_4$, the Turán-coloring criterion of Fox–Wigderson) do not apply to the triangle-free, girth-5, 3-chromatic Petersen graph. It is a natural test case, between odd cycles (common) and graphs containing $K_4$ (uncommon).
issues: Original 'determine the constant' rewritten as the commonness question; if P is common the constant is 2^{-14}. Checks: P has no K4, so Thomason's obstruction does not apply. Its smallest even subgraph with min degree 2 is C6, and t(C6,U)>=0, so P passes the first local-commonness test. Turán colorings give 32-560 times the random value. A random search over 2- to 4-step graphons found nothing below 2^{-14} (best 1.035x). Found no paper settling P.

title: Is the measure of the hyperbolic real quadratic parameters computable?
W: For real c between −2 and 1/4, the map x ↦ x²+c has an attracting cycle for an open dense set of c, yet the chaotic parameters have positive length (Jakobson). Is the total length of the parameters with an attracting cycle a computable number? It can be approximated from below by listing windows, but no known method approximates it from above.
M: Let $H=\{c\in[-2,1/4]:\ x\mapsto x^2+c\text{ has an attracting periodic orbit}\}$. Is the Lebesgue measure $\lambda(H)$ a computable real number? ($H$ is open and its components can be certified by interval arithmetic, so $\lambda(H)$ is lower semicomputable; Jakobson's theorem gives $\lambda(H)<9/4$.) Equivalently: is the measure of the set of stochastic (Collet–Eckmann) parameters lower semicomputable?
why: This is a basic constant of one-dimensional dynamics, and no rigorous nontrivial upper bound on it is known. Computer-assisted Jakobson-type schemes (Luzzatto–Takahashi; Golmakani–Koudjinan–Luzzatto–Pilarczyk) certify expansion, not stochasticity. A positive answer would give a certified two-sided estimate; a negative one would be a striking non-computability result for a natural dynamical quantity.
issues: Checked the reduction: the stochastic set is a countable union over CE constants of intersections of finite-time conditions. That makes each piece upper semicomputable, which is the wrong direction, so the answer does not follow from the obvious approach. Golmakani et al. (2020) certify an escape-time property on about 90% of a parameter piece but explicitly do not prove stochasticity. Found no paper on computability of λ(H). Statement is precise (parabolic parameters have measure zero).

title: Integrability of the egg-crate torus
W: Put the surface z = ε sin x sin y over a flat square torus. Show its geodesic flow is never integrable, however small the bumps are.
M: For $\varepsilon>0$ let $g_\varepsilon$ be the metric on $\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^2$ induced from the graph $z=\varepsilon\sin x\sin y$, i.e. $g_\varepsilon=dx^2+dy^2+\varepsilon^2(\cos x\sin y\,dx+\sin x\cos y\,dy)^2$. Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ the geodesic flow on $T^*\mathbb T^2\setminus0$ has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of the Hamiltonian (for example, by showing positive topological entropy).
why: Kozlov's theorem rules out first integrals that are analytic in ε for generic trigonometric perturbations of the flat torus. Proving non-integrability at each fixed ε, uniformly down to ε→0, needs control of exponentially small splitting at resonances. This is an explicit test of that gap.
issues: Wrote out the metric explicitly. The ε-analytic (Poincaré–Kozlov) version follows from Kozlov because the Fourier spectrum of the perturbation is not on a line. The fixed-ε statement for all ε>0 seems open but is quite specific. By Paternain/Taimanov, positive topological entropy would be enough.

title: Icosahedral monotile
W: Find a single 3D tile that fills space and forces five-fold, icosahedral symmetry in every tiling, or prove that no such tile exists.
M: Does there exist a compact set $T\subset\mathbb R^3$ homeomorphic to a ball, which tiles $\mathbb R^3$ by congruent copies, such that for every tiling $\mathcal T$ by copies of $T$ the hull $\Omega(\mathcal T)=\overline{\{\mathcal T+x:x\in\mathbb R^3\}}$ (local topology) satisfies $R\,\Omega(\mathcal T)=\Omega(\mathcal T)$ for every $R$ in some icosahedral rotation group $G\cong A_5$? (This forces strong aperiodicity, by the crystallographic restriction.)
why: Icosahedral quasicrystals are modeled by tilings with two or more prototiles (Ammann rhombohedra, Danzer tetrahedra). The new 3D aperiodic monotiles, such as Socolar–Taylor and recent strongly aperiodic examples, all live in crystallographic orientation classes. A single tile that forces non-crystallographic symmetry would close that gap.
issues: Made precise: 'icosahedral symmetry in its hull' now means hull invariance under an A5 rotation group. Ball topology added to exclude degenerate disconnected tiles. Recent 3D strongly aperiodic monotiles (e.g. arXiv 2609.19214) use cubic frames, with symmetry order at most 24, so they do not answer this. Even the 2D analogue (a monotile forcing 5- or 10-fold symmetry) seems open and is the more natural first target, which keeps this at B.

title: Proof complexity of the sensitivity theorem
W: Huang proved that any set of more than half the corners of the n-cube contains a corner with at least √n neighbours inside the set. Write this as a propositional formula with one variable per corner. Do polynomial-size proofs exist in resolution, cutting planes or sum-of-squares, measured against the 2^n variables?
M: Let $N=2^n$, $d=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil-1$. $\mathrm{SENS}_n$ is the CNF on variables $x_v$ ($v\in\{0,1\}^n$) plus sequential-counter variables encoding $\sum_v x_v\ge 2^{n-1}+1$, together with the clauses $\neg x_v\vee\bigvee_{u\in U}\neg x_u$ for every $v$ and every $(d+1)$-set $U$ of neighbours of $v$ (size $N\cdot n^{O(\sqrt n)}=N^{1+o(1)}$). It is unsatisfiable by Huang's theorem. Does $\mathrm{SENS}_n$ have refutations of size $N^{O(1)}$ in (a) resolution, (b) cutting planes, (c) sum-of-squares of degree $O(\log N)$? Lower bounds $2^{N^{\Omega(1)}}$ are equally of interest.
why: Huang's proof is a short spectral argument, interlacing for a signed adjacency matrix. Asking whether weak proof systems can capture it tests how much linear algebra cutting planes and SOS can simulate. It belongs to the programme of locating famous combinatorial theorems in the proof-complexity hierarchy.
issues: Checked the sizes: the formula has size N^{1+o(1)}, and Huang's bound gives unsatisfiability exactly at d=ceil(sqrt n)-1. Part (a) is probably 'no' for routine pigeonhole/matching reasons: even the d=0 case (an independent set larger than N/2) is a matching-type principle that is hard for resolution. That case is easy in cutting planes via a perfect matching. So (b) and (c) are the real content, and the W wording should stress them. Found no prior work on this.

title: Lane–Emden with a shift
W: Replace u² in the five-dimensional Lane–Emden equation by the square of u at a shifted point. Are there still no positive solutions?
M: Let $e\in\mathbb R^5\setminus\{0\}$. Does there exist a positive $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^5)$ with $-\Delta u(x)=u(x+e)^2$ for all $x\in\mathbb R^5$?
why: For $p<(n+2)/(n-2)$ (here $2<7/3$), Gidas–Spruck shows $-\Delta u=u^p$ has no positive entire solutions. Their proof, like moving planes, relies on the nonlinearity being local, so a shifted nonlinearity tests which Liouville methods survive nonlocal coupling.
issues: 1D analogue is trivially impossible (positive concave on R is constant). The superharmonic-inequality threshold n/(n-2)=5/3<2 does not settle it, and |x|^{-3} decay is not excluded by crude integral estimates. Found no literature on shifted-argument Lane–Emden. The choice of n=5, p=2 is arbitrary; the natural version is 'for all n≥3, 1<p<(n+2)/(n-2)'.

title: Hat Ising universality
W: Magnets on a hat tiling should behave at their critical point exactly like magnets on a square grid. Prove it.
M: Let $G$ be the planar graph whose vertices are the tiles of a fixed hat tiling (Smith–Myers–Kaplan–Goodman-Strauss), with edges between tiles sharing a boundary segment. Consider the ferromagnetic nearest-neighbour Ising model on $G$ with uniform coupling $J=1$. Prove that there is a critical $\beta_c$ (independent of the tiling in the hull), and that as $\beta\to\beta_c$ the spontaneous magnetization, susceptibility and correlation length obey $M(\beta)\asymp(\beta-\beta_c)^{1/8}$, $\chi(\beta)\asymp|\beta-\beta_c|^{-7/4}$, $\xi(\beta)\asymp|\beta-\beta_c|^{-1}$.
why: Rigorous 2D Ising universality is known for isoradial graphs at Z-invariant weights and for periodic graphs. Uniform couplings on an aperiodic, non-isoradial graph are not covered. The hat graph is a canonical such test, and numerics (Matsubara–Suzuki) support universality.
issues: Original M did not say which graph, which couplings, or which definitions of the exponents. Fixed: tile-adjacency graph, uniform J, and asymptotics up to constants. Existing work is Monte Carlo only, with ν and β assumed rather than fitted. This is an instance of the broader open problem of universality for quasiperiodic planar Ising models.
